# 2 Maccabees Chapter 1 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 1 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_001_page_001.jpg

---

## Preamble

Chapter 1 comprises two letters from the Jerusalem Jewish community to the Jews in Egypt, urging them to celebrate the festival of the temple rededication (Hanukkah). The first letter (vv. 1–9) was written in 143 BCE; the second (vv. 10–36) contains the miraculous fire narrative connected with Nehemiah. EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA show convergence on structure and theology, with disagreements on register and the rendering of key terms.

---

**1** The Jews in Jerusalem and Judea, together with the council of elders and Judas, to their brothers and sisters — the Jews throughout Egypt: greetings and true peace.

**2** May God bless you and keep his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.

**3** May he give each of you a heart devoted to worshiping him and to doing his will wholeheartedly and eagerly.

**4** May he open your hearts to his law and his commandments, and may he grant you peace.

**5** May he hear your prayers, be reconciled to you, and never abandon you in a time of evil.

**6** And now we ourselves are here, praying for you.

**7** In the reign of Demetrius, in the one hundred and sixty-ninth year, we wrote to you about the severe distress that came upon us in those years — from the time when Jason and his associates apostatized from the holy land and the kingdom,

**8** and burned the gate and shed innocent blood. We prayed to the LORD and were heard; we offered sacrifice and grain offering; we lit the lamps and set out the bread of the Presence.

**9** And now take care to celebrate the Feast of Booths in the month of Chislev.

**10** In the one hundred and eighty-eighth year — from the people in Jerusalem and Judea, from the council of elders and from Judas — to Aristobulus, teacher of King Ptolemy and himself of the anointed priestly line, and to the Jews in Egypt: greetings and health.

**11** Having been rescued by God from grave dangers, we give him great thanks, since we engaged such a king in battle.

**12** For it was he who drove out those who had arrayed themselves against the holy city.

**13** For when the general arrived in Persia with an apparently invincible army, they were cut to pieces in the temple of Nanea, by the treachery of Nanea's priests.

**14** For Antiochus came to the place with his Friends, on the pretense of marrying her, in order to take possession of its great wealth as a so-called dowry.

**15** When the priests of Nanea set out the money and Antiochus entered the inner shrine with only a small retinue, the priests shut the doors of the temple.

**16** Opening a hidden trapdoor in the ceiling, they hurled stones down on the leader and his men, cut them to pieces, and threw the heads out to those waiting outside.

**17** Blessed in all things be our God, who has delivered up those who acted with impiety.

**18** Since we will be celebrating the purification of the temple on the twenty-fifth of Chislev, we have thought it necessary to let you know, so that you also may celebrate the Feast of Booths and the feast of the fire — the fire given when Nehemiah, who rebuilt the temple and the altar, offered sacrifices.

**19** For when our ancestors were being led captive to Persia, the devoted priests of that time took fire from the altar and secretly hid it in the hollow of a dry cistern, where they guarded it carefully so that the place was unknown to anyone.

**20** After many years had passed, when it pleased God, Nehemiah — sent back by the king of Persia — dispatched the descendants of those priests to recover the fire. When they reported that they had found no fire, only a thick liquid,

**21** he ordered them to draw it out and bring it. After the sacrificial materials had been set in place, Nehemiah commanded the priests to sprinkle the wood and the offerings with the liquid.

**22** When this was done, and some time had passed, and the sun that had been hidden by clouds shone out, a great fire blazed up, so that all were filled with wonder.

**23** While the sacrifice was consumed, the priests offered prayer — Jonathan leading and the rest responding, with Nehemiah joining them.

**24** The prayer was this: "O LORD, LORD God, Creator of all things — you who are awesome and strong and righteous and merciful, you who alone are King and full of grace,

**25** you who alone are the great Provider, you alone are just and almighty and eternal, you who rescue Israel from every evil, who made our ancestors your chosen people and consecrated them:

**26** accept this sacrifice for all your people Israel; preserve your heritage and make it holy.

**27** Gather together our scattered people; free those who are enslaved among the nations; look with favor on those who are rejected and despised; let the nations know that you are our God.

**28** Punish those who oppress and who treat us with contemptuous pride.

**29** Plant your people in your holy place, as Moses proclaimed."

**30** Then the priests sang the hymns.

**31** After the sacrifice was consumed, Nehemiah ordered the remaining liquid poured out on large stones.

**32** When this was done, a flame blazed up — but it was extinguished by the brilliant light shining back from the altar.

**33** When the matter became known, the king of Persia was informed that in the place where the exiled priests had hidden the fire, water had appeared, with which Nehemiah and his associates had purified the sacrificial materials.

**34** The king investigated, had the site enclosed, and declared it sacred.

**35** He responded generously to those with whom he exchanged gifts.

**36** Nehemiah and his associates called this substance "Nephthar," which means "purification," but most people call it "naphtha."

---

## Translator's Notes

- **v. 7, "apostatized"**: EMET uses "defected," LOGOS "apostatized," PNEUMA "betrayed." SOPHIA adopts "apostatized" as most precise for religious defection.
- **v. 10, "council of elders"**: Greek *gerousia*. SOPHIA retains this formal translation. PNEUMA's "our council" is idiomatic but accurate.
- **v. 14, "Friends"**: Greek *philoi* — Seleucid court title for royal companions. Capitalized per convention.
- **v. 18, "Feast of Booths in Chislev"**: The text deliberately links the temple purification festival (Hanukkah) to Sukkot, presenting it as a kind of winter Sukkot. Both festivals involve fire and light.
- **v. 36, "naphtha"**: The wordplay on *Nephthar* (purification) and "naphtha" (petroleum) is a feature of the original Greek text.
